title: A Study of Students' Readiness to Learn Calculus paper: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40753-015-0013-y
author: Craig Barton
summary: This Tips for Teachers research summary covers Carlson, Madison and West's development and validation of the Calculus Concept Readiness (CCR) instrument, a 25-item multiple-choice test designed to diagnose whether students have the foundational reasoning abilities needed to succeed in calculus before they start the course. Using both large-scale CCR test data and qualitative student interviews, the researchers found CCR scores correlate strongly with later calculus grades, and identified specific precalculus weak points — most notably covariational reasoning, a genuine process view of functions, proportional reasoning, angle measure, and the sine and cosine functions. The study's most striking finding is diagnostic rather than statistical: many students are passing their first semester of calculus despite carrying severe, identifiable deficiencies in the underlying reasoning abilities and knowledge base the subject depends on. Barton draws out the practical use of the CCR as a placement and instructional-targeting tool — rather than a generic readiness check, it points precalculus teachers toward the specific concepts (angle measure and the sine function stand out as particular weak spots) that most need reinforcing before students move on. The implication for teachers more broadly is that surface-level pass rates in a prerequisite course can mask exactly the conceptual gaps that will resurface, and compound, in the next course up.
points: The 25-item Calculus Concept Readiness (CCR) instrument correlates strongly with subsequent calculus grades, making it a genuinely predictive diagnostic rather than a generic entry quiz.
Many students are passing first-semester calculus despite carrying 'severe deficiencies' in foundational reasoning and knowledge — a pass rate can mask exactly the gaps that matter most.
Covariational reasoning and a genuine process view of functions (not just static function evaluation) are singled out as the core reasoning abilities calculus readiness actually depends on.

Angle measure and understanding of the sine function were identified as specific, widespread precalculus weak points — giving teachers a concrete target for remediation rather than a vague 'brush up on trig' instruction.

The CCR is framed as a tool for improving both placement decisions and precalculus instruction itself, by revealing exactly which conceptual gaps instruction needs to close before students attempt calculus.
quotes: This research article investigates the readiness of college students for calculus, revealing significant weaknesses in foundational knowledge and reasoning abilities.
The authors developed the Calculus Concept Readiness (CCR) instrument, a 25-item multiple-choice test, to assess these areas and predict student success in calculus.

Analysis of CCR results from a large sample of students demonstrates a strong correlation between CCR scores and calculus grades, highlighting specific precalculus concepts where improved instruction is needed.
The CCR instrument assesses covariational reasoning, understanding the function concept, proportional reasoning, angle measure, and sine and cosine functions.
The study found that many students did not have a strong understanding of angle measure or the sine function.

These data in combination with our examination of the percentages of correct CCR answers further supports that many students are taking and passing first semester calculus with severe deficiencies in their reasoning abilities and knowledge base.
